title: Radiocarbon Dating – The Profile of Nancy Athfield
sourceHeading: Radiocarbon Dating: A Profile of Nancy Athfield

source.filename: Practice 50  IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 1.pdf

paragraphs.text: Have you ever picked up a small stone off the ground and wondered how old it was? Chances are, that stone has been around many more years than your own lifetime. Many scientists share this curiosity about the age of inanimate objects like rocks, fossils and precious stones. Knowing how old an object is can provide valuable information about our prehistoric past. In most societies, human beings have kept track of history through writing. However, scientists are still curious about the world before writing, or even the world before humans. Studying the age of objects is our best way to piece together histories of our prehistoric past. One such method of finding the age of an object is called radiocarbon dating. This method can find the age of any object based on the kind of particles and atoms that are found inside the object. Depending on what elements the object is composed of, radiocarbon can be a reliable way to find an object’s age. One famous specialist in this method is the researcher Nancy Athfield. Athfield studied the ancient remains found in Cambodia. Many prehistoric remains were discovered by local people in Cambodia. These objects were thought to belong to some of the original groups of humans that first came to Cambodia. The remains had never been scientifically studied, so Nancy was greatly intrigued by the opportunity to use modern methods to discover the true age of these ancient objects.

Athfield had this unique opportunity because her team, composed of scientists and filmmakers, were in Cambodia working on a documentary. The team was trying to discover evidence to prove a controversial claim in history: that Cambodia was the resting place of the famous royal family of Angkor. At that time, written records and historic accounts conflicted on the true resting place. Many people across the world disagreed over where the final resting place was. For the first time, Athfield and her team had a chance to use radiocarbon dating to find new evidence. They had a chance to solve the historic mystery that many had been arguing over for years.

Athfield and her team conducted radiocarbon dating on many ancient objects found at Angkor Wat. She found that the history of Angkor extended back to at least 1620. Historical records suggested that the remains of the Angkor royal family were much younger, so the evidence cast considerable doubt on the identity of the ancient remains. The research ultimately raised more questions: if these were not the remains of the royal family, whose remains were interred at the site? Athfield’s team left Cambodia with many questions unanswered. Since the study, further remains have been unearthed at Angkor Wat, and these may prove to be the true remains of the royal family. Athfield hoped to return one day to continue her research.

Athfield’s early career was highly unconventional. She did not begin as a scientist and initially took any work she could find to pay her bills. Most positions were low-paid jobs or brief community-service opportunities. She worked regularly but did not know which path she would ultimately follow. Eventually, a friend suggested that she pursue a degree at a nearby university. Although doubtful about her qualifications, Athfield applied and was accepted. There she met Willard Libby, the inventor of radiocarbon dating. She attended his class and soon gained hands-on research experience, realising that science was her passion. After graduating, she quickly found work at a research institution.

After university, Athfield’s scientific career blossomed. She married, and her husband obtained a job at the prestigious organisation GNS. Athfield joined him there and became a laboratory manager. Her PhD research examined when a species of rat first appeared in New Zealand. She produced original work and identified several flaws in methods used by New Zealand laboratories, showing that the subject’s diet accounted for errors in earlier research. Her peers regarded her as an expert, and her judgement was widely respected. She had come a long way from working odd jobs; her career was finally taking off.

Laboratory science was not Athfield’s only interest. Rather than settle permanently in New Zealand, she broadened her expertise, entered anthropology—the study of human societies—and became a qualified archaeologist. During this flourishing archaeological career, she joined the well-known Cambodian project. Even after the filmmakers ran out of money and left Cambodia, Athfield remained to continue the research.

In 2003, the film ended without firm conclusions, but Athfield continued to study the ruins of Angkor Wat. The work was often delayed by insufficient funding and government paperwork, yet she remained committed to completing it. Finally, she made a breakthrough by compiling a database of radiocarbon dates for materials found in Cambodia. As a newcomer, she lacked a complete understanding of Cambodian geology, making the achievement even more difficult. Through determination and ingenuity, Athfield completed the database. Although many doubted that she would finish, her work remains an influential contribution to Cambodia’s geological sciences. Radiocarbon dating will continue to be a valuable research method, and Athfield will be remembered as one of the first people to apply it to the ancient ruins of Angkor Wat.
